summary: Explains the long-standing tradition of Independent Submissions, RFCs that do not come out of the IETF standards process. Such documents serve useful functions for the wider community, and this memo describes how people can submit them to the RFC Editor and how they are reviewed and published.

eli5.summary: Most Internet notes come from one big club, but anyone can offer a note on their own. This paper explains how you hand yours in and how the editor decides whether to print it.

questions: how to submit an independent rfc
who decides whether an independent submission is published
what does the iesg review for independent submissions
subtitle: How documents that do not come from the IETF get reviewed and published as RFCs.

tldr.problem: The RFC Series predates the IETF and has always carried documents that are not products of the IETF standards process, but the way those documents are reviewed and published was not written down.
tldr.mechanism: Independent Submissions go straight to the RFC Editor, who arranges reviews, asks the IESG only for a non-technical check for conflicts with IETF work, and makes the final decision on publication.
tldr.outcome: The RFC Editor, not the IETF, keeps the final say, so Independent Submissions can stay independent. This memo was later updated by RFC 5744.

today: RFC 4846 is an Informational RFC published in July 2007 and has been updated by RFC 5744. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Independent Submissions Exist
sections.content:
The RFC Series goes back 38 years as of this memo, while the IETF was then celebrating its 21st anniversary. Everything published before the IETF existed, and for some years after, would be called an Independent Submission today. When the IETF began publishing its work as RFCs, it did so knowing the RFC Editor was an independent publisher, and it chose to keep using the same series.

The memo separates Independent Submissions from documents of formal IETF and IAB groups (the IAB, the IRTF and IETF working groups) and from individual submissions, which are written by individuals but go through the IESG under Area Director sponsorship.
sections.eli5: The collection of Internet notes is older than the club that now writes most of them. Some notes still come from outsiders, and this paper says how that works.

sections.title: What Independent Submissions Are For
sections.content:
The memo lists many uses, among them discussion of Internet technologies that are not on the IETF agenda, a bridge between academia and IETF engineering, informational publication of vendor-specific protocols, and experience reports. It also lists satire, meeting notes, editorials, eulogies and technical contributions.

One use gets special weight: critiques of alternatives to IETF Standards-Track protocols. The memo says the chance of such critiques is an important check on the IETF's standards processes. Documents that working groups considered but did not standardize may also come this way, though the memo says they should normally go through the IETF document stream.

Because of these roles, the review process should be largely independent of the IETF. A submission that is an alternative to, or in conflict with, an IETF Standard or Standards-Track proposal must clearly say so.
sections.eli5: People send in all sorts of things: new ideas, jokes, meeting notes, or a friendly argument against the big club's plans. The editor wants to keep that door open.

sections.title: Submitting and Reviewing a Document
sections.content:
Authors first post the document as an Internet-Draft, then send a request to the RFC Editor, noting any earlier community review and the category wanted (Informational or Experimental). Documents made in IETF processes are preferred to go through the IESG, and come this way only if a working group or the IESG declines them.

The RFC Editor then runs an initial check, arranges one or more reviews (possibly by the Editorial Review Board), and returns a written summary of the reviews to the author. Authors may rebut a review. A preponderance of favorable reviews should normally lead to publication.

If the author is unhappy, they may ask for additional reviews, or in exceptional circumstances ask the IAB to review. The IAB is not required to do so, and its review is not an appeal. The RFC Editor may reject a document that does not meet the technical or editorial standards of the series, and the final decision always rests with the RFC Editor.
sections.eli5: You hand in your draft, a few readers comment, and you can answer them. The editor makes the final call, and you can ask for more readers if you disagree.

sections.title: The IESG Conflict Review
sections.content:
Normally after the RFC Editor tentatively decides to publish, the document goes to the IESG with a relatively short timeout. The memo says this evaluation is not technical. It covers the issues in RFC 3932 and should focus on conflicts or confusion with IETF process and attempts to end-run working group activities.

The RFC Editor posts a notice on its Web site that the document is under IESG review. If the IESG finds issues, it may recommend explanatory text. It may also ask for publication to be delayed. The agreement then in place let the IESG ask for a delay of up to six months, renewable twice, for a total of 18 months. If the IESG asks that the document not be published, the RFC Editor considers the request with the IESG's justification. Either party may ask the IAB for an advisory opinion.
sections.eli5: Before printing, the editor shows the note to the big club only to check it does not trip over the club's own work. The club can ask to wait a while, but it cannot overrule the editor.

sections.title: The Editorial Board and Review Transparency
sections.content:
The RFC Editor appoints and maintains the Editorial Review Board, which gives advice and reviews, much like the editorial boards of journals. Members serve at the pleasure of the RFC Editor, who asks the IAB for suggestions and comments but keeps the final decision on appointments to protect independence.

Reviews go to the authors, usually with the reviewer's name, though anonymity is granted on request. After a decision, the RFC Editor may post the full set of reviews and rebuttals. An author who objects must act in a timely way, generally within 14 days of the notice of intent. The memo notes that the best way to dissent from an RFC is generally another RFC.
sections.eli5: A panel of helpers reads submissions with the editor. Reviewers can stay anonymous if they ask, and authors get a short window to say no before reviews are posted.

sections.title: Rights and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Section 8 repeats material from BCP 78 so that all Independent Submission rules are in one place. Contributors grant the IETF Trust and the IETF a license to publish the document as an Internet-Draft and, for an RFC, an irrevocable license in perpetuity to copy, publish, display and distribute it, plus rights for translations and, unless disallowed in the notices, derivative works.

The Security Considerations section says the memo describes an administrative and publication procedure and has no specific security implications.
sections.eli5: When you hand in a note you also give permission for it to be printed and copied. This paper is only about rules for paperwork, so it has no security worries.
